events.title: Lyle Brewer “Learning Curve” Album Release
about: Lyle Brewer returns to the Lizard Lounge November 12th for the release of his latest album "Learning Curve"
$25 adv/$30 door
Lyle Brewer is a guitarist and songwriter from Massachusetts who incorporates the worlds of fingerstyle, jazz and folk into a style all his own.

A professor at Berklee College of Music and a sideman to artists such as Lori McKenna, Ryan Montbleau and Neighbor, Brewer has earned a reputation as one of the most skilled instrumentalists and composers of his generation.

What separates Lyle from other guitarists, however, is what he doesn’t play. Not just another instrumental technician, Brewer’s music is always in service to the song, creating a rich and sophisticated quality both on record and in performance.

The Boston Globe describes his music as “thoughtful, artfully composed instrumentals”, while USA Today writes, “Brewer’s technical ability is staggering — each note both runs into the next and seems to stand out on its own. The melodies take the place of lyrics. The songs tell stories without words.”

On his 13th solo album, “Learning Curve”, that same balance between technical mastery and narrative-based storytelling is on full display. This new album is a collection of 10 poignant songs that draw inspiration from Nick Drake, Joni Mitchell, The Beatles and Antonio Carlos Jobim.

Whether on nylon string or electric guitar, Brewer has a strong ability to communicate his ideas. You don’t need to be a guitarist to dive into Brewer’s instrumentals. He lets the music do the talking.

Originally hailing from right around the corner in Brighton, MA – The Brighton Beat is a unique and engaging spectacle for all ages. A huge band playing epic horn funk with a full horn section, epic percussion, and non-stop foot stomping grooves. With influences ranging from classic New Orleans brass band Funk to Classic 70’s Afrobeat this is a dance party not to miss!. Performing up and down the East coast since 2010, the band has developed a style of performance that uniquely engages the audience and is fun for the whole family. Positive, uplifting, danceable music is a trademark of The Brighton Beat sound. Instrumental songs that feature room for the horn section to improvise anchor the band’s set, but the show often includes guest vocalists, audience participation, group sing-a-longs and even the occasional circus act. Welcome to your new favorite band/family.

Three things bind this quartet together: friendship, a love of jazz and funk, and a shared sense of humor. In the 2010s, Bassist Jameson Stewart, organist Ben Blanchard, drummer Patrick Dalton, and guitarist Sam Crawford formed a close personal and musical rapport working together as sidemen in various styles. It wouldn’t be long until they tried playing their own instrumental music as a quartet. Today, QuadraPeg brings joy and vitality to their compositions and improvisations, always with a solid groove, camaraderie, and a touch of the absurd.

events.title: ONELOUDDRAWING
about: Jonah / onelinedrawing with a full band doing Far’s Tin Cans on its 30th anniversary, plust stuff from New End’s Thriller & the new onelinedrawing album RAINBOWMACHINE ARTIST BIO: onelinedrawing is Jonah Matranga of Far, Gratitude, New End Original, and more. On September 18, Iodine Recordings will release RAINBOWMACHINE, the new album from onelinedrawing. The album was produced by Jay Maas. It’s the loudest, wildest onelinedrawing record yet. The tracks above are from the album. There will also be the first full-band onelinedrawing shows in forever in September and October, celebrating the 30th anniversary of Far’s TIn Cans With Strings To You, the 25th anniversary of Thriller, and of course the new album.

Jonah started onelinedrawing in 1998, just as his first band, post-hardcore / emo misfits Far, was breaking up. The first onelinedrawing releases were a cassette on POPROCKIT, a label started by Kevin Seconds (7 Seconds). Then came the Sketchy EPs, first self-released, then in various forms on various indie labels (Crank, Revelation, Corrupted Image). During that time, onelinedrawing pioneered sliding-scale pricing for downloads and merch, monthly crowdfunded patronage (eventually released as the Always New albums), and Unique Recordings. During that time, onelinedrawing toured with and/or released music with Rival Schools, The Juliana Theory, Coheed & Cambria, Dashboard Confessional, Murder By Death, The Weakerthans, Jimmy Eat World, and more.

onelinedrawing’s most recent studio album is Tenderwild, on Iodine Records. Iodine also recently released Sketchbook, a collection of early onelinedrawing recordings 1999-2001. onelinedrawing also has two albums (VISITOR and THE VOLUNTEERS) still on Jade Tree / Epitaph. Over 30 years, several projects, dozens of albums, hundreds of songs, and thousands of shows, Jonah Matranga has influenced countless artists: Deftones, Frank Turner, Thursday, My Chemical Romance, Walter Schreifels, and Chris Carraba. Jonah has also been featured on tracks by Deftones, Thursday, Fort Minor, Lupe Fiasco, Kimya Dawson, and many more.
onelinedrawing is the thread that runs through it all.

Hunter Flynn is a Kentucky-born singer-songwriter and visual artist whose work resonates with emotional honesty and a deep connection to Appalachian culture. Raised in Pulaski County, Flynn’s path to music and art wasn’t a straight line—it was forged through adversity and personal transformation. In early 2022, after surviving a life-altering car accident, he decided to fully embrace his creative passions, launching a music career rooted in authenticity, vulnerability, and soul.

Drawing inspiration from the landscapes and stories of Appalachia, Flynn blends elements of folk, country, soul, and gospel into a genre-defying sound he calls Appalachian Soul Music. His lyrics, often reflective and raw, tell stories of pain, redemption, resilience, and identity—underscored by his powerful vocals and minimalist arrangements. These qualities are showcased in his debut EP, Appalachian Soul, released in May 2023, which quickly gained traction for its emotional depth and stripped-back sincerity.

Featuring AYEL, Belen, DÁN, and Aydan Hill, the night brings together four independent artists with distinct musical backgrounds and perspectives, moving between folk, pop, alternative, and cinematic influences. Through personal songwriting, expressive vocals, and immersive arrangements, each artist offers a different take on identity, vulnerability, and human connection.

AYEL is a French singer-songwriter, producer, pianist, and film composer based in Boston. Her sound blends pop, R&B, soul, rock, electronic, and cinematic influences, bringing together intimate songwriting and expansive arrangements. Currently studying Film Scoring at Berklee College of Music, she moves between writing for her own project, collaborating with other artists, and composing for film. Her music explores vulnerability, self-expression, and the search for connection, with the intention of making listeners feel seen, heard, and less alone. Her recent work includes the release “Better” and the placement of “The Story Never Ends” in All American.

Belen is a francophone German-Filipino-American folk-adjacent singer-songwriter and multidisciplinary artist based in Boston. Known for her acoustic textures and tender songwriting, she draws on her multicultural upbringing and visual-art background to create music rooted in vulnerability and emotional storytelling. Born in Berkeley, California, and raised between a rural village in southern France and Germany, she brings a distinctive perspective to her work. She taught herself guitar at 16 before moving to Paris to study music, and now attends Berklee College of Music on a full-tuition scholarship. Her cover of “Ma Meilleure Ennemie” from Netflix’s Arcane reached over three million views across platforms, and she is currently preparing her upcoming EP, From Above.

Originally from northern Italy, his musical journey has taken him from festivals and live performance to Berklee College of Music, where he expanded his craft in music production, recording, and engineering. about: Join us at The Rockwell for a curated evening of Folk Rock and Alt-Country, celebrating Jake Klar’s album release, with special guests Noble Dust and Hayley Sabella.

Years Go Through Me Now, a new collaborative album by singer-songwriter Jake Klar and folk-rock trio Blue Ranger, is a quiet triumph of such glimpses. In its nine songs and two interludes, I hear the motions of weathered hands, the gentle rush of country roads, the laughter of old friends and the silence of rumination — the quilt of dreams and doings we call a life.

GoldFlakePaint describes Klar’s music as “An urgent meeting of folk, roots and good old rock and roll that carries with it an unbreakable spirit.” A fixture in New England’s folk scene, Klar has toured nationally, played festivals including Otis Mountain Get Down and FreshGrass, and supported the likes of Cut Worms, Antwaun Stanley, and Al Olender.

Klar has spent the past decade working as a letterpress printer, art store clerk, bartender, carpenter, illustrator, graphic designer, musician (touring DIY on his own and as a member of Prewn and Hannah Mohan), live sound engineer, merch guy, and custodian. His songwriting, from the misty-eyed title track to the down-home boogie-woogie of “Driving Home Through the Country” (here recast murmurously from an earlier electric version), dwells in a rustic realm borne by his crackling voice and hearthside acoustic guitar. “That Forever” is a haunted, fragmented road-movie that emerges from its dust like a lost Basement Tapes recording, while the last-call piano ballad “Louisa” wouldn’t sound amiss on After The Gold Rush.

events.title: Captivating Swaras
about: $20 admission / $10 students & seniors / 5pm doors / seated & standing Captivating Swaras returns to the Lilypad this Saturday! This time we have a very special interactive performance from harmonium master Kedar Naphade, accompanied by Pranav Ghatraju on tabla. come to hear his wonderful playing as well as for an interactive audience-inclusive session where you can learn about this wonderful instrument, how it’s played, ask questions, and learn! this amazing event should not be missed by anyone interested in harmonium and indian instruments.

Kedar Naphade is a globally renowned harmonium soloist and accompanist in Indian Classical, Semi-Classical and Devotional music, including Bhajan, Kirtan and Chanting. He founded The Harmonium Institute, a not-for-profit that teaches harmonium to students of all levels, ages and locations. He was trained for over three decades by Harmonium Maestro Late Padmashri Pt. Tulsidas Borkar and Vidushi Smt. Padmavati Shaligram-Gokhale. In a 30+ year career, Kedar has performed across India, the US, Canada and Europe, at venues including Carnegie Hall, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Lincoln Center, the Smithsonian and The World Harmonium Summit (Bangalore). His music has been broadcast on NPR and on other radio stations in the US and UK.

Pranav Ghatraju began learning tabla at age 5 under Dr. Nishikant Sonwalker. He now studies with Ustad Shabbir Nisar, son of Tabla Nawaaz Ustad Shaik Dawood Khan of Hyderabad. Pranav has accompanied artists and performed solo across the US and India since a young age. He received a New England Conservatory scholarship to its World Rhythm boot camp (2007), was the youngest recipient of INDIA New England’s 20 Under 20 award (2010), and won the under-15 mega finals at Swarganga’s Crescendo 2011. In 2023, INDIA New England named him a “Rising Star.”

A fine, high-powered tenor saxophonist with a tone influenced by John Coltrane, a mastery of chord changes, and a strong musical imagination, Jerry Bergonzi has long had an underground following in the Boston area. He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. He has since led several groups (including two called Con Brio and Gonz) and recorded for the Plug, Not Fat, Red, and Blue Note labels. — By Scott Yanow, AllMusic Continuing Every Monday at 8:30pm Lineup subject to change

about: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 10pm doors / 10:30 start / seated The Fringe originally formed back in 1971 by tenor-saxophonist George Garzone, bassist Richard Appleman, and drummer Bob Gullotti as an outlet for their free jazz improvisations, The Fringe have entertained and enlightened Boston area jazz audiences for over 50 years. Bassist Appleman left the band in 1985 to become Chairman of the Bass Department at Berklee College and was replaced by veteran bassist John Lockwood.
Bob Gullotti passed away in 2020 and is remembered as one of the greatest jazz drummers of his generation. Francisco Mela, now on drums, graciously fills the space Bob left behind.

Along with their impressive tenure with The Fringe, Garzone, Lockwood, and Mela are in great demand as session players and have played with many of the greats of contemporary jazz. Joe Hunt is a jazz drummer, educator, author, and historian. In the early 1960s, Joe Hunt performed and recorded alongside the late NEC Distinguished Artist-in-Residence Emeritus George Russell, with releases on Decca and Riverside. Hunt joined The Stan Getz Quartet in 1964, recording several releases on Verve, then was a member of the Bill Evans Trio from 1966-1967. The remainder of the 1960s found Hunt performing or recording with several other jazz luminaries including Chet Baker, Eric Dolphy, Dizzy Gillespie, Dexter Gordon, Charles Mingus, Bob Brookmeyer, and the late Herb Pomeroy.

In the 1970s and 1980s, Hunt was a member of The National Jazz Ensemble, led jazz groups with John Scofield, Mike Stern, and Santi Debriano, and toured with quartets of Red Rodney and Hal McKusick. The 1990s, and beyond, have included membership in The Smithsonian Jazz Masters Orchestra, with former NEC president Gunther Schuller, performances with Kenny Burrell, Joe Lavano, Joanne Brackeen, and Tal Farlow, as well as recordings with the Bert Seager Quintet, and also, Trio. Hunt is the author of the 1994 book 52nd Street Beat, which is a historical look at jazz drummer greats from 1945 to 1965.

events.title: Jerry Bergonzi Quartet
about: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 8:30 start / 8pm doors / seated Jerry Bergonzi, Tenor Saxophone Luther Gray, Drums Plamen Karadonev, Piano Sean Farias, Bass Special Guest, Trumpet Double-click to edit...

A fine, high-powered tenor saxophonist with a tone influenced by John Coltrane, a mastery of chord changes, and a strong musical imagination, Jerry Bergonzi has long had an underground following in the Boston area. He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. He has since led several groups (including two called Con Brio and Gonz) and recorded for the Plug, Not Fat, Red, and Blue Note labels. — By Scott Yanow, AllMusic Continuing Every Monday at 8:30pm Lineup subject to change

events.title: Nondualism Trio presents Nosferatu Funk
about: $15 admission / 7pm doors / 7:30 start / seated & standing The Boston-based progressive jazz group Nondualism Trio presents "Nosferatu Funk" at the Lilypad! Featuring Mark Tipton (trumpet), James Heazlewood-Dale (bass), and Paul July Joseph (drums), Nondualism Trio will be playing original works, including Mark's compositions from their upcoming album, "Nosferatu Funk." The set will include: "Paraconsistent Refractions," "Walk-A-Seven Ghost Dance," "Lithospheric Waltz," "Cosmic Dust Groove Thang," "Into the Wilderness," "Slow Burn," "Nosferatu Funk," a pair of musical "Mantras," and more! Expect deep grooves, musical complexity, and synergistic ensemble playing.

Nondualism Trio is a Boston-based progressive jazz trio that includes Mark Tipton on trumpet, James Heazlewood-Dale on bass, and Paul July Joseph on drums. Mark is originally from Maine, James is originally from Australia, and Paul is from Haiti. Nondualism Trio was formed in 2025 and in February 2026 they recorded their first album at Q Division Studios in Cambridge, MA, featuring Mark’s original compositions. They have recently performed at The Lilypad in Cambridge, The Drake in Amherst, and NEC’s Pierce Hall.

The ensemble’s name, Nondualism Trio, is derived from the Indian philosophy that views reality as an interconnected whole, devoid of dualistic thinking, whereby awareness can be experienced beyond conceptual thought. It is this state of mind that Nondualism Trio seeks to embody when they are performing together: collectively open-minded in their improvisations to carry the music wherever it wants to go, and free from judgements and intuited mental road-blocks. Their music is both structured and open.

The three members of Nondualism Trio are all rising talents in jazz, and are all active musicians on the Boston scene, seasoned touring musicians, and devoted teachers (Mark at NEC, James at Brandeis, and Paul through his private studio). James and Mark have recently toured Turkey, Cypress, and the Northeastern US with Mehmet Ali Sanlıkol and both his jazz quintet and classical Turkish music ensemble, DÜNYA, while Paul and Mark have recently toured New England. They enjoy connecting with diverse audiences and inspiring young musicians.
Mark Tipton is a Boston-based jazz trumpeter, composer, and educator who has recently been appointed as Assistant Chair of Jazz Studies at NEC. He has recently…

about: $10 admission / 7pm / seated show Jesse Gallagher began living above the Lilypad in 2006, just a few blocks from where his grandfather grew up on Inman st. At the time Jesse was in the middle of what would be about a decade of regular touring, performing & recording with his psychedelic rock band Apollo Sunshine. The band was featured in the New York Times, Rolling Stone, Spin & shared the stage with legendary acts Wu-Tang Clan, Toots & The Maytals, The Flaming Lips & Dr. Dog. Jesse has been involved with the Lilypad for 20 years and the full time talent booking agent since 2013.

Breaking Bad used Jesse’s song “We are Born When We Die” (2008) to dramatic effect. “Today is the Day” (2005) was in international Nike commercials while his “Singing to the Earth to Thank Her For You” was used in a large GAP campaign. Gallagher has collaborated, recorded & performed extensively w/ Sam Cohen, Willy Mason, Lilys, Nick Nicely, Doug Tuttle & Edan. Gallagher is a certified Yoga & Meditation teacher and hosts classes at the Lilypad & online. Since 2018, he has released 40 pieces of instrumental music which have been used in millions of YouTube videos ranging from NBC NY to Tesla and most recently a string of viral videos by Emma Chamberlain. Gallagher has a very active YouTube channel, making lots of psychedelic music videos and building a community of mindful listeners.

Steve Fell is a guitarist, composer, and educator whose performing and recording career over the last twenty five years has reached across the boundaries of jazz, experimental, funk, free form improvisation, rock, electronic, reggae/calypso, hip-hop, psych, and many others.
He co-leads the groups Clear Audience, Quantum Banditos, Dome Room, and Astronomico, leads a trio under his own name, and collaborates with numerous bands and artists.

events.title: Fall Writer’s Round
about: $15 at the door / $10 advance / 4:30pm doors / all ages Stories told through song. A Nashville-style writers' round featuring indie-pop/folk Berklee songwriters: Brigham Cooper, Hadley Johnson, Mariam Kubursi, and Maya Salafia.

Hadley Johnson is a 20-year-old indie pop/folk singer-songwriter from Cape Elizabeth, Maine. She grew up playing a medley of instruments and began writing songs at 13. Since then, she has performed at many venues throughout Portland and Boston. In January 2026, she released her debut EP, “The Idea of Me,” which tells stories of young love and loss, and includes themes of coming-of-age and moving on. Throughout her music, Hadley prioritizes sharing authentic stories through heartfelt lyrics and intimate arrangements. In doing so, she encourages listeners to explore their own vulnerability, and take comfort in knowing they aren't alone.

Maya Salafia is an indie-pop singer-songwriter based in Boston, Massachusetts. Known for her striking mix of raw emotion, killer hooks, and honest lyrics, Maya’s sound is the soundtrack for life’s messy moments. Maya Salafia released her debut album, Girl Like Her, on February 6th on all streaming platforms. Exploring topics surrounding falling in love and self-discovery, Girl Like Her brings a new level of vulnerability and truth to the indie-pop scene. Maya’s music has been featured in numerous music review blogs, radio shows, and websites. She has performed live at various clubs, coffeehouses, and festivals throughout New England.

Brigham Cooper is a folk artist who blends surrealist lyricism with enchanting soundscapes and finger-style guitar. Hailing from Rutland, VT, their music tackles personal themes of identity and the human experience, with nods to their home and the people who have molded them into the musician they are today. Their song "To Die For," which speaks on the fluidity of gender and the balancing act of self-expression and personal safety, placed 3rd in Berklee's "Songs For Social Change" competition.

Mariam Kubursi is a singer-songwriter from Palo Alto, California, blending folk, Americana, and soft pop into a true and timeless sound. Mariam’s music connects listeners to the unique and inevitable experiences of life— nostalgia, love, heartbreak, and everything in between. Her wild honesty and addictive melodies paired with her light-hearted guitar riffs transport listeners to a vivid…

events.title: Emissary Quartet: [moment]um
about: $20 admission / $10 for students / 5pm doors / 5:30 show <a href=" class="sqs-block-button-element--small sqs-button-element--tertiary sqs-block-button-element" data-sqsp-button > Get Tickets Emissary Quartet’s debut album and concert program, [moment]um, is inspired by the Japanese concept of jo-ha-kyū, a structure that reflects the natural flow of progression: beginning slowly (jo), accelerating through development (ha), and culminating in a swift and powerful conclusion (kyū). This theme of movement, time, and motion is brought to life through contemporary works by living composers, Jennifer Higdon, Kai-Young Chan, Sung-Hyun Yun, Nicky Sohn, Heike Beckmann, and Herman Beeftink. Each composer uses the unique textures and timbres of the flute and auxiliary flutes, to evoke a sense of continuous transformation. Each piece within the album highlights various facets of moments and motion, from the meditative, gradually unfolding soundscapes of the opening movements to the more dynamic, rhythmically intricate passages that create a palpable sense of urgency and energy. The living composers draw upon a wide range of influences, blending minimalist repetition with more expansive, lyrical phrasing to reflect [moment]um, while exploring the capacity of sound to depict both literal and abstract forms of motion.

Emissary Quartet is committed to cultivating connection and opportunity through dynamic performances and residencies that empower musicians and foster community. EQ has presented at various conventions, including the National Flute Association, and has received numerous grants and honors, including from New Music USA and The Fromm Foundation.

EQ continues to curate a catalog of new works that fully exploit the dynamic expressive capabilities of four flutes together. The ensemble held an International Call for Scores throughout the 2016-2017 season and received over 190 submissions from composers across the globe. In 2025, EQ released their debut album, [moment]um, with a newly commissioned work by composer Nicky Sohn. EQ continues to develop fruitful collaborative relationships with composers to further music of their generation and make flute quartet music a significant part of the sound landscape of today.
EQ’s passion for collaboration extends beyond the bounds of music alone. In 2023, EQ presented Emissary Artists, an event of live art and music at Box13…

events.title: Music from the Dark Side
about: $15 admission / 7:30 doors / standing / all ages Three music projects explore moody aspects of folk, darkwave and ritual, shamanic sounds and vocals. Featuring Winds of Alluria, Shadowmerge, and Ajda the Turkish Queen.

Enchanting female vocals from Eurasian Shaman Khaluna Kam. Together with Totem Faehy's incredible throat singing and natural connection to animism, he brings an element sound balance. Heavy ritual ancestral sounds, authentic shamanic vocals, throat and overtone singing, and kulning. Their unique vocal abilities create a memorable journey of sound rooted in ancient traditions of ritual and lore.

Shadowmerge is the latest project from veteran Boston guitarist Doug Vargas and singer/poet Marlene Tholl. This ambient darkwave collaboration explores the evolution of ethereal alternative rock, poetry, and song — a moody mix of Vargas' atmospheric guitar and Tholl's haunting vocals and emotionally charged spoken word. This Lilypad performance marks the release of their new EP, E-Life, which grapples with the complex challenges of modern life through haunting soundscapes and post-rock textures. Following their previous release, Weight of Forever, E-Life marks a shift toward a more driving, ethereal sound.

Ajda the Turkish Queen is a singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist who typically performs on guitar and mandolin. Currently focused on solo endeavors including her forthcoming second solo album “Only Child", she will perform some of those very autumnal tunes at this show. She is founder of bands such as Black Fortress of Opium and the Ronnie James Dio tribute AjDIO. Influences include artists like Little Jimmy Scott, Nick Cave, PJ Harvey, Nico, Ute Lemper, Siouxsie Sioux, Ella Fitzgerald, and more, as well as the lonesome voices of Turkish muezzins.

events.title: Bruce Gertz Quintet
about: $15 / $10 students / 7pm doors / 7:30 start / seated Bruce Gertz Quintet Jeff Stout, trumpet Rick DiMuzio, tenor Russell Hoffmann, piano Bruce Gertz, bass Gary Fieldman, drums Double-click to edit...

Bruce's new solo recordings are like meditations that vibrate in the solar plexus and resonate through your being. His command of the instrument and imagination are an elixir for being transported to the pure music channel. Bravo Bruce - Jerry Bergonzi Every morning, world-renowned jazz bassist, composer, and educator, Bruce Gertz, makes himself a cup of coffee and sits at the baby grand piano of his Melrose, MA living room. Surrounded by quirky plants, records of his esteemed inspirations, and albums of his own, Gertz composes something every day, regardless of the day’s events ahead. He says, "Sometimes I only get a short idea but that can be the seed of a beautiful composition." His counterparts applaud him for his restless commitment to self-improvement.

Gertz is known for his superb mastery of the upright bass and was named “Outstanding Bassist” by Boston Music Awards. What some fans don’t know is that he grew up playing electric bass from the age of 14 and still plays (and teaches) the electric quite often. His extraordinary contribution to music education has earned him multiple recognition awards from The International Association of Jazz Educators and the Jazz Education Network. He has been serving as a Professor of Bass at Berklee College of Music since 1976. Additional educator credits include serving on the advisory board of the International Society of Bassists and as an adjudicator at the Clark Terry UNH Jazzer's Festival.

Gertz has performed and recorded with such artists as Gary Burton, Jerry Bergonzi, John Abercrombie, Joey Calderazzo, Kenny Werner, Mick Goodrick, Kurt Rosenwinkel, Billy Hart, Bill Frisell, Bob Berg, George Cables, Gil Evans, Tom Harrell, Jon Hendricks, Diane Schuur, Dave Brubeck, George Garzone, Mike Stern, Larry Coryell, Joe Lovano, Cab Calloway, Maynard Ferguson, Count Basie and many others.

He is an author of six books and contributing editor to Bass World Magazine. As a bandleader, Gertz has recorded more than twenty albums. His latest quartet release received four stars in Downbeat, December, 2017.

events.title: Meg Gehman
about: $20 admission / 5:30 doors / 6pm start / seated / all ages Meg Gehman brings her soulful voice and original music, a mash-up of soul, blues, folk, and rock, as she promotes the first single, The Dawn, from her forthcoming album, LoveSister.

Meg Gehman is a Nashville-based Americana Soul artist. Her songs are real and intimate; an amalgam of folk, blues, funk, soul and rock. A captivating singer and songwriter, Meg is a warm and engaging performer whose lyrics often pay tribute to the the resiliency of the human spirit and the power of love over fear. While Meg has her own style, comparisons can be drawn to artists such as Bonnie Raitt, Susan Tedeschi, Joan Osborne, Annie Lennox, Rickie Lee Jones or Indigo Girls.

events.title: Bog Fancy Magazine Presents: the HAG ATTACK COMMENCEMENT
about: $10 admission / 7pm doors / 8pm start / all ages Bog Fancy Magazine features their twisted authors reading strange tales to improvised soundscapes by haunted sound artists like Mute City and Death Shepherd. Followed by full sets from hip-hop zombies Z.W.A., coven-wave band Do Whatever Die Whenever, and horror-synth video butcherer NO GRAVE.

Z.W.A is the futuristic variants of Mac and TD (of Big Digits) and Karen (of UV Protection) who find themselves woken up from their eternal graveyard slumber by nuclear bombs. In their undead forms, they have found each other, started making heavy beats and witty rhymes, and decide to go back in time to warn the music appreciators of today about the upcoming apocalypse. Their sound—a fusion of hip-hop horror, dance floor grit, and theatrical flair—is inspired by the likes of Gravediggaz, Blondie's "Rapture," and Michael Jackson's Thriller video. They are the zombie screaming rapping prophets the world never asked for.

Crystal shop loiterers DO WHATEVER DIE WHENEVER are the guitar and synth duo of CC OhNo-Bates and Ulf Rattenhelfer. Their Voices from the Dark EP swerves from dancey dark-wave to punky deathrock, while covering topics of high strangeness, pseudo-esoterism, and philosophical pessimism.
NO GRAVE is a dread-synth multimedia onslaught of electronic scores performed over warped and smeared vintage slasher-flick video-collage.

BOG FANCY is a regular magazine featuring WEIRD STORIES and WEIRD ILLUSTRATIONS, and when performed live it also features WEIRD MUSIC from the area's best soundscapesmiths. Embrace every feeling a person can have, as long as it's SPOOKY, SAVAGE, and STRANGE.

about: $5 - 15 sliding scale admission / 4 - 7pm / all ages We're excited to be welcoming the community into our space to play and listen to music together. The Lilypad Jazz Jam is open to instrumentalists of all levels, we only ask that you come prepared to play at least one or two well known Jazz Standards in the commonly played key. We have Nic Adams hosting and leading the band to get the night started. Come early, you won't want to miss their performance!

Nic Adams is a multi-instrumentalist, performer, composer, educator, and luthier based in Boston, MA. Specializing in saxophone, drums, guitar, bass, and north Asian folk music, their music pulls from a long list of traditions, from John Coltrane to punk rock and Tuvan throat singing. With this wide array of influences, Nic seeks to create music that synthesizes many different musical points into a cohesive and unique form. Finding common grounds among musical cultures and using them as jumping-off points for new compositions or improvisations is at the core of Nic’s work. Nic is currently pursuing a Master’s at Longy School of Music, gigs in the greater Boston area, and spends their free time building hybrid Tuvan/western traditional instruments.

about: $25 at the door / $20 in advance / $15 students and seniors / 7:30 doors / seated <a href=" class="sqs-block-button-element--small sqs-button-element--tertiary sqs-block-button-element" data-sqsp-button > Get Tickets Lafayette Gilchrist featuring special guest and Cambridge native, Cecil Brooks of the Sun Ra Arkestra.

Lafayette Gilchrist’s music draws on the span of jazz history from stride to free improvisation, along with inspiration from hip-hop, funk, and Washington D.C.’s unique go-go sound. His work thrives on making surprising connections between styles and influences, boldly veering from piledriver funk to piquant stride, vigorous swing to hip-hop swagger, contemplative abstraction to deep-bottom grooves. Gilchrist is the pianist in the Sun Ra Arkestra, has toured extensively with David Murray, and his compositions have graced the soundtracks of David Simon’s acclaimed series The Wire, The Deuce, and Treme.

Gilchrist has performed with Cassandra Wilson, Macy Gray, Oliver Lake, Andrew Cyrille, Orrin Evans, Paul Dunmall, Hamid Drake, William Parker and many more. Gilchrist’s second solo recording, 2019 “Dark Matter” which muses on the elusive and mysterious matter that ties the universe together, landed on numerous critics best of lists.

Gilchrist returns to The Lilypad, where he played for a standing room only crowd in 2022, for a performance featuring a special guest appearance by Cambridge native and fellow member of the Sun Ra Arkestra, Cecil Brooks on trumpet.

about: $20 admission / $15 for students and seniors / 1:45 doors / 2pm start New Music for the 21 piece Jazz Orchestra by resident composers David Harris, Darrell Katz, Bob Pilkington and Mimi Rabson.

The Jazz Composers Alliance was founded in 41 years ago to support, develop and promote the art of music composition in the jazz idiom. The JCA Orchestra was founded to realize that goal, and it has been a fixture on Boston’s creative music scene ever since its first performance in December 1985. The JCA Orchestra has released 12 critically acclaimed CDs. Wheelworks was on Downbeat’s Best of 2016 list. The group has performed (and on a few occasions, recorded with) an illustrious group of guest performer/composers, including Sam Rivers, Julius Hemphill, Dave Holland, Maria Schneider, Henry Threadgill, Steve Lacy and Oliver Lake. Drawing on influences that span the history of jazz and the world's musical traditions, the JCA Orchestra has brought together a huge palette of sounds, structures and concepts. This group has premiered well over 125 pieces. Our concepts include extended forms, group improvisation from a variety of approaches, notated and not notated music, and striving to combine composition and improvisation in new ways.

The 21-piece JCA orchestra a string trio, a vocalist, as well as a full-time flute player, and French horn, we’re not a typical big band, We have lasted since 1985, and it’s because we have a like-minded group of people who love making music, who are committed to stretching boundaries, and write and perform with joy and passion. JCA performances have variety, adventure, and a great communal feel.

“The band plays with drive and vitality. the soloists responding with imaginative fire to the charts and the ensemble. This is contemporary big band music of a very high order, written and played with considerable skill and integrity”

about: $14 advance / $18 door / 11pm - 1am / seated & standing <a href=" class="sqs-block-button-element--small sqs-button-element--tertiary sqs-block-button-element" data-sqsp-button > Buy Tickets Having opened for Wayne Shorter and toured internationally alongside Snarky Puppy and Sungazer, Sirintip comes to Boston for her first headlining performance in the city, celebrating the release of her new EP White Lilies, out October 30. events.title: Allan Chase Quartet ft. Sheryl Bailey
about: $15 admission / 6pm doors / 6:20 start / seated Jazz classics and originals by Chase and Bailey.

Allan Chase is a saxophonist and composer who has performed jazz and improvised music since 1974 with his own groups and as a member of the Lewis Nash-Allan Chase Duo (1979-80), Your Neighborhood Saxophone Quartet (1981-2018), Prima Materia with Rashied Ali (1992-2000), the Steve Lantner Quartet with Joe Morris and Luther Gray, the Bruno Råberg Quartet and Tentet, and the Ayn Inserto Jazz Orchestra. He appears as a soloist on over sixty jazz and improvised music recordings, several rock and classical recordings, and several movie scores.

Chase began teaching at Berklee in 1981 and served as chair of Ear Training there (2008-21). He has also taught at Tufts and NEC, where he served as chair of Jazz Studies, dean of faculty, and chair of Contemporary Improvisation, and continues to teach jazz history courses.

events.title: Joe Hunt Group
about: $15 admission / Start 8:30pm / Doors 8pm / Seated Show Modern jazz played by Boston's best jazz musicians.

Joe Hunt is a jazz drummer, educator, author, and historian. In the early 1960s, Joe Hunt performed and recorded alongside the late NEC Distinguished Artist-in-Residence Emeritus George Russell, with releases on Decca and Riverside. Hunt joined The Stan Getz Quartet in 1964, recording several releases on Verve, then was a member of the Bill Evans Trio from 1966-1967. The remainder of the 1960s found Hunt performing or recording with several other jazz luminaries including Chet Baker, Eric Dolphy, Dizzy Gillespie, Dexter Gordon, Charles Mingus, Bob Brookmeyer, and the late Herb Pomeroy.

In the 1970s and 1980s, Hunt was a member of The National Jazz Ensemble, led jazz groups with John Scofield, Mike Stern, and Santi Debriano, and toured with quartets of Red Rodney and Hal McKusick. The 1990s, and beyond, have included membership in The Smithsonian Jazz Masters Orchestra, with former NEC president Gunther Schuller, performances with Kenny Burrell, Joe Lavano, Joanne Brackeen, and Tal Farlow, as well as recordings with the Bert Seager Quintet, and also, Trio. Hunt is the author of the 1994 book 52nd Street Beat, which is a historical look at jazz drummer greats from 1945 to 1965.

Mark Pinto - alto saxophone, formerly years with the Buddy Rich band John Lockwood – bass, formerly with Joe Henderson, Lee Konitz, current Fringe member Yuka Hamano Hunt – piano, voice, arranger Joe Hunt – drums, formerly with George Russell, Stan Getz, Jim Hall, Dexter Gordon, and Bill Evans We pay tribute to a special composer or performer at most performances. Recent shows have included: Burt Bacharach, Ahmad Jamal, Bill Evans, and Gigi Gryce. Future shows will include the music of Paul and Carla Bley, and arranger, Johnny Mandel.

events.title: Bert Seager's Standard Deviation
about: $15 suggested / $5 with Student ID / 6:30pm start / seated The jazz quintet Standard Deviation, led by pianist and composer Bert Seager, is a tight, two-horn, hard-bop combo that plays his arrangements of jazz standards alongside his own singable originals. The music offers plenty of room for the band to open up and interact. Their special chemistry makes it obvious why sharing jazz in an intimate club like the Lilypad remains such a compelling communal experience.

Bert Seager, pianist, composer, recording artist, and educator, has led performances in international jazz festivals in Canada, Peru, Bulgaria, Jordan, Ecuador, Israel, China and Japan. events.title: Eliza Edens & Nora Meier
about: $12 advance / $15 day of show / 9:15 doors / 9:30 music / all ages Brooklyn-based songwriter Eliza Edens celebrates the release of their latest record 'Death Drive.' Local songwriter Nora Meier supports.

Eliza Edens is a Brooklyn-based songwriter who writes songs that dance inside the white-hot intersection of pleasure and pain. Bold and sincere, their songs are like antique cameo necklaces–snapshots of tenderness, worn close to the heart. A palette of punchy electric guitars and drums, gentle keys, and flourishes of saxophone and electronic percussion accent Edens’ voice as they sing of lovers & lilacs, grief & gratitude, and Freud’s “death drive.” Chameleonic in nature, Edens touches corners of pop, rock, folk, and country–with their voice as the glue that binds each genre foray together into a commanding sound.

Edens came up initially on the DIY songwriter circuit–playing self-booked tours of small clubs and listening rooms on the quiet success of 2020’s Time Away From Time and 2022’s lush acoustic-fingerpicked We’ll Become the Flowers. They earned praise from outlets such as Paste Magazine, The Nashville Scene, Spill Magazine, and Americana UK while incessantly touring across America. Cutting their teeth on the road eventually paid off as Edens won runner-up at the esteemed Telluride Troubadour Songwriting competition in 2024. The veneer of a quiet songster singing breezy Nick Drake-esque melodies was quickly dashed after Edens lost their mother in late 2024 after a long journey with early-onset dementia. After releasing 2025’s lo-fi collection of voice memos it’s your birthday & you’re gorgeous with no fanfare or promotion, Edens disappeared from touring for the better part of a year. Some say Edens went out to New Mexico to find god. Others say Edens turned into a butterfly and floated south to greener pastures. Edens will say that they continued to find hope in writing songs.

Newly molded by the black hole of grief, the singer reemerges this fall with their first record in 4 years. Death Drive is the sound of someone finding themself while also losing control. Heavy and light, black and neon-tinged, the album is a masterful achievement of contemporary indie rock, poignantly moving through the landscape of grief while also foisting joy, love, and humor up to the light.

events.title: Reclaiming My Heartbeat
about: A live storytelling experience about transplant, resilience, and patient advocacy.
A second chance at life was only the beginning.

In Reclaiming My Heartbeat, Kyreé Miller brings humor, honesty, and hard-earned perspective to the stage as he shares his journey through five open-heart surgeries, two LVADs, and ultimately, a heart transplant.
But this isn’t simply a story about surviving. It’s about what happens afterward—reclaiming your body, finding your voice, advocating for yourself, and building a life that feels like your own again.
Part live storytelling experience and part audience conversation, the evening will include Kyreé’s signature humor, an interactive Q&A, and time to connect after the show.

Whether you’re a patient, caregiver, healthcare professional, or someone rebuilding after life changed unexpectedly, Reclaiming My Heartbeat is a celebration of resilience, self-advocacy, and learning how to truly live after survival.
Presented by Kyreé Miller and Five Heartbeats Productions LLC.

Dana Cooper's 32nd Release "The Ghost of Tucumcari" was Voted #1 Album of 2024 on Americana Highways Readers Poll. This album features Lyle Lovett, Hayes Carll, Susan Gibson, Darden Smith, Shake Russell and more. It takes listeners on a stirring musical journey across genres from Folk and Rock to Country and Americana. Charting #7 on Folk Chart & #9 on Alt Country Radio Charts. Dana Cooper is a poetic songwriter, an insightful storyteller, and a rousing musician whose performances engage & inspire audiences around the world. Central to Cooper's unique artistry is his ability to connect with audiences through his authentic stories, sense of humor and warm stage presence.

The studio band consisting of legendary players -"The Section" with Leland Sklar & Russ Kunkel AKA "The Immediate Family." Since then, he worked with Shake Russell in Texas, releasing several albums together and performing on "Austin City Limits." Dana has also collaborated with several established artists - Kim Carnes (Betty Davis Eye's), Don Henry, Hal Ketchum, Kim Richey, Tom Kimmel & more. His 2022 CD "I Can Face The Truth" garnered much praise and attention, charting on 5 different Radio Charts.

Tonight’s theme is… Frenemies: five-minute stories about the razor-thin line between friend and foe. The relationships that drive you up the wall or the connections you can’t quite quit. events.title: Gary Higgins
about: Octafish Events presents: Psych-folk legend GARY HIGGINS live at the ROOTED Armory Cafe in Somerville Free-folk enigma Gary Higgins entered the popular consciousness more than three decades after his music career ground to an abrupt halt when the reissue of his 1973 cult classic, Red Hash, became a cause célèbre in the summer of 2005. A new generation of psych-folk devotees including Current 93's David Tibet and Ben Chasny of Six Organs of Admittance had discovered the album sang its praises. In late 2004, the Drag City label finally located Higgins and reissued Red Hash.

about: Join us for an unforgettable Night To Be Heard— delicious food, stories, dance, music, and voices from beheard.world's talented artists!

Dance. Poetry. Film. Music. Food. Community.

Join the dancers, poets, filmmakers, educators and youth and community members of beheard.world for an evening celebrating the power of art to bring us together—and the voices that deserve to be heard.

events.title: The Bowery Presents Pokey LaFarge
about: Pokey LaFarge is coming to Arts at the Armory on November 10, 2026 to celebrate the release of his new album, 'Rent Money'. Grab your tickets now!

For two decades, Pokey LaFarge has walked his own effortlessly cool road as an exceptionally iconoclastic troubadour – forthright, genuine, and markedly keen to put it all out there. Rent Money now sees him pushing forward yet again in what can be safely declared his finest collection to date, both as an heartfelt expression of personal experience and as no-nonsense social commentary. With its twanging guitars, plucky rhythms, and undeniably captivating melodies, the album soars and swings, its joyous refrains belying the inescapable undercurrent of constant worry and angst that permeates these troubled times. As always, the Illinois native deftly traverses the genre boundaries, seamlessly integrating the myriad strains of 20th-century American music with a freewheeling command of earnest songcraft, inspired performance, and subversive creativity. Rent Money stands tall as an indisputable high-water mark for Pokey LaFarge – a defining collection from a one-of-a-kind artist of rare ingenuity and uncommon candor, now as ever, determinedly crafting a sure-footed brand of deeply human music all his own.

events.title: The Bowery Presents Liana Flores
about: Doors open at 7:00 PM · Show begins at 8:00 PM
“This record is the story of the country girl moving to the city,” Liana Flores says. “It’s bossa nova meets pop, inspired by the people, relationships and glamour of city life.”

Since the release of her acclaimed 2024 debut album Flower of the soul, British-Brazilian singer-songwriter Liana Flores has been at the forefront of a bossa nova revival. Drawing on the ‘60s sound of genre pioneers like Joao Gilberto alongside pop songwriting, Flores combines the dual aspects of her cultural heritage to create an emotive sound.

Following extensive tour dates across North America, Asia and Europe, Flores now returns with a new EP, And so it goes…, that expands her palette to encompass the playful and ebullient experiences of moving from her rural hometown in Norfolk to St. Andrews before coming to London. The result is a six track collection that shifts between finger-picked guitar and gossamer bossa vocals of “So it goes” to the upbeat funk inflections of the heavy-grooving love song “So mysterious”, the Carole King-influenced folk storytelling of “Here to stay,” and the sprightly, glittering pop melodies of “Silvershoes.”

“These songs were informed by my experiences living in the city and touring for the first time. I grew up and studied in small towns with nature in my surroundings, so that’s what came naturally in terms of lyrics. With So it goes, the lyrics are more centred on human connection, and I wanted to explore a part of my identity that’s more playful and matter-of-fact. I also wanted to challenge myself to write songs with strong melodies that would be fun to sing or to get ready to.”

Raised by an immigrant Brazilian mother and British father in East Anglia, Flores first began learning music while listening to ‘80s and ‘90s bossa nova artists like Bebel Gilberto and Leila Pinheiro alongside Top 40 pop radio. In her late teens, she picked up a guitar and started emulating finger-picked bossa nova guitar chords by ear, first covering Tom Jobim standards, then writing her own songs combining the bossa guitar style with her own introspective lyrics, expressing loneliness, self-doubt, and endurance.

“Music is the way I best communicate and connect with the world, through the listener, collaboration with fellow musicians, and the guidance of my musical forbears. I'm particularly drawn to the use of sophisticated…

events.title: An Ocean (Re)Introduction
about: Emmy Award-winning storyteller and explorer Richard Vevers invites you to see the ocean in a completely new way.

Best known for his work on the Netflix documentary Chasing Coral and for pioneering Google Street View underwater, Vevers now leads Room 71 at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, an initiative transforming how we understand and communicate ocean science.

In this talk, Vevers challenges what we think we know about the ocean. Drawing on insights from leading oceanographers and explorers, he reveals how human perception often distorts our understanding of the vast and dynamic world beneath the surface.

Through compelling stories and imagery, he reintroduces the ocean as it truly is—complex, surprising, and deeply connected to our lives. You may never look at the ocean or our planet the same way again.

events.title: Studio Ossidiana—Giovanni Bellotti and Alessandra Covini
about: Studio Ossidiana—Giovanni Bellotti and Alessandra Covini Part of the MIT Fall 2026 Architecture Lecture Series.

Presented with the Architecture and Urbanism Group Studio Ossidiana is a design practice based in the Netherlands, working across scales to create spaces, objects, exhibitions, and installations at the intersection of architecture, design, art, and landscape. The studio’s projects include experimental playgrounds for children and adults, floating gardens inhabited by birds, outdoor kitchens, land art pavilions on water, to be explored and cultivated by humans and other species.

Led by Alessandra Covini and Giovanni Bellotti, with Klaas van der Molen joining the studio in 2025, Studio Ossidiana collaborates with international institutions including the Centre Pompidou and the National Museum in Oslo. The studio’s work has been presented at the Venice Architecture Biennale (2021–2023), Milan Triennale (2022), Shenzhen Architecture Biennale (2022), Istanbul Design Biennial (2021), Chicago Architecture Biennial (2021), and Bruges Triennial (2024).

Alongside their design practice, Giovanni and Alessandra teach at international universities, including HEAD Genève (Haute école d’art et de design), where they lead a course exploring the relationship between plants and interiors.

Studio Ossidiana’s work has received numerous awards and distinctions, including the Prix de Rome (2018), the Netherlands’ oldest award for designers under 35; the Italian Architecture Under 35 Award (2023); and nominations for the European Union Prize for Contemporary Architecture / Mies van der Rohe Award (2024, 2026).
This lecture will be held in person in the Sidara Auditorium (W41- 1216) and streamed online on YouTube.
Lectures are free and open to the public. Registration is required.

events.title: Our Own Language / Lang a nou — Book Launch & Public Conversation
about: Celebrate MIT Prof. Michel DeGraff’s new book _Our Own Language / Lang a nou_. Introductory remarks, conversation & book signing.
OUR OWN LANGUAGE / LANG A NOU A Book Launch & Public Conversation with Michel DeGraff and Haynes Miller.
Introduced and Moderated by M. S. Vijay Kumar.
What happens when children are denied the right to learn in the language they know best?
What becomes possible when communities reclaim their own languages as tools for knowledge, education, human rights, dignity, democracy, liberation and nation-building?

Our Own Language: Harnessing the Power of Kreyòl and Other Mother Tongues for Education and Liberation Lang a nou: Kreyòl ak lòt lang manman se zouti pou edikasyon ak liberasyon Drawing on Haiti’s revolutionary history, the struggle for Kreyòl in education, and the predicament of post-colonies around the world, Our Own Language / Lang a nou challenges a belief with deep roots in colonial history, namely the belief that some languages — and, by implication, some people — are more worthy of access to knowledge and power than others.

For this special evening, linguist, activist and author Michel DeGraff will introduce some of the stories and ideas that led him to write the book, then he and Haynes Miller will engage each other and the audience in a conversation about language, education, inequality and the possibilities afforded by Liberatory Linguistics.
The conversation will be introduced and moderated by M. S. Vijay Kumar.
Books will be available for purchase and signing.
Come celebrate our languages and imagine an education where every child counts.
The event is free and open to the public.

events.title: MIT / French Library Author Series: Before I Forget with Anne Pauly
about: Anne Pauly is a Paris-based French writer and winner of the Prix du Livre Inter and Prix Robert Walser. Her debut novel, Before I Forget, was also shortlisted for the Prix Goncourt, Prix Femina, and Prix Wepler. Before turning to fiction, she worked as a journalist and wrote on music, feminism, queer culture, and literature.

In Before I Forget, Pauly recounts the aftermath of her father’s death and the complicated task of mourning a man who was at once a self-taught philosopher and romantic, and an alcoholic whose violence marked his family. As Anne sorts through his belongings and prepares his funeral, she tries to reconcile these contradictory versions of the man she has lost. Told with wit and tenderness, the novel is a tragicomic exploration of grief, family, class, and the complicated bonds between parents and children.

The conversation will be moderated by Bruno Perreau, Cynthia L. Reed Professor of French Studies at MIT and a specialist in contemporary French literature and culture, critical theory, and politics. He is the author of thirteen books, including Queer Theory: The French Response and, most recently, Spheres of Injustice: The Ethical Promise of Minority Presence (MIT Press, 2025).

events.title: Undoing Gender in French Literature
about: The French modernist canon has been read has a key site for sexual dissidence, but what about gender? In this talk, Mat Fournier presents his book, Dysphoric Modernism, and questions the entanglements of the modern gender binary with state power and colonial history. Through readings of Gide, Genet, Colette, and others, Fournier explores how narratives of sexual dissidence both deconstruct and reinforce mutually exclusive definitions of masculinity and femininity and racial discriminations. In this web of contradictions, modern gender appears as inherently dysphoric, imposing untenable positions and perpetuating systemic hierarchies. Ultimately, tracking the dysphoria traversing modernist writings offers a perspective into gender’s complicity with historical and contemporary fascisms, and offers strategies of resistance.

events.title: Eleni Sikelianos and Julie Carr: the William Corbett Poetry Series
about: Born into a family of bohemians, poets, tree workers, ne’er-do-wells, visionaries, and smalltime sort-of hustlers, Eleni Sikelianos is a poet, writer, collaborator, and “master of mixing genres” (according to TimeOut). Kirkus has called her most recent book, Memory Rehearsal (City Lights, 2026; the third book in her trilogy of ancestral encounters) “a moving family memoir and a triumph of cultural archaeology.” Deeply engaged with ecopoetics, her work takes up urgent concerns of environmental precarity and ancestral lineages. Her tenth book of poetry, Your Kingdom came out in 2023. Her work has been translated into a dozen languages, and she has in turn translated works by Jacques Roubaud, Sabine Macher, and, most recently, Mohamed Leftah. She grew up in earshot of the ocean, in small coastal towns near Goleta, and has since lived in San Francisco, New York, Paris, Athens (Greece), Boulder (Colorado), and Providence.

Julie Carr’s recent books are The Garden (Overflow, book one); Underscore; Mud, Blood, & Ghosts: Populism, Eugenics, & Spiritualism in the American West. Her co-translations of Leslie Kaplan’s Excess–The Factory and The Book of Skies, were published by Commune Editions & Pamenar Press. Books two and three of Overflow will be published sequentially over the next few years. She lives in Denver where she co-runs Counterpath, teaches at the University of Colorado Boulder, & hosts the podcast “Return the Key: Jewish Questions for Everyone.”

events.title: From Brooklyn to the North Pole: An Illustrated Journey with Photographer Leonard Sussman
about: Experience the polar regions through the lens of photographer Leonard Sussman.

What does it take to create a photograph at the edge of the world? Join photographer Leonard Sussman for an illustrated talk exploring the extraordinary landscapes and experiences of the polar and sub-polar regions. From the Arctic to Antarctica and everywhere in between, his work captures some of Earth's most remote locations.

Since 2014, Sussman has embarked on over a dozen expeditions to some of Earth's most remote and breathtaking locations: the Svalbard archipelago, Alaska, Greenland, Patagonia, Antarctica, and the sub-Antarctic islands of New Zealand and Australia. His camera has captured these fragile, stunning environments in ways that challenge and inspire.

Sussman will share stunning imagery from his polar expeditions, reveal the challenges of photographing in extreme environments, and discuss his book, From Brooklyn to the North Pole: 52 Days on the USCG Icebreaker Healy. Copies of Sussman's book will be available for purchase following the event.
A limited number of free tickets are available for full-time students with ID. Please reach out to museumregadmin@mit.edu.

events.title: Artist Talk: Hao Jingban
about: The List Visual Arts Center will host an artist talk in celebration of the opening of Hao Jingban: I Witness followed by an opening reception.
Artist, Hao Jingban, will be in conversation with doctoral student in East Asian Film and Media Studies at Harvard University, Huirong Ye.

This exhibition marks Hao’s first major US museum solo, featuring recent work centered on I Witness (2025), a three-channel installation that takes up the embodied residue of the COVID-19 pandemic: four participants move slowly through a well-lit apartment, their images punctuated by stories of loss—an older woman who sleeps alone and rises to clean her refrigerator, a group of young people pacing an open field.

Hao Jingban lives and works between Yunnan Province, China, and Berlin, Germany. She received an MA from the University of London and BA from Goldsmiths College. Recent solo exhibitions include Mori Art Museum, Tokyo (2025); Matadero Madrid (2020); OCT Contemporary Art Terminal, Xi’an, China (2019) and recent group exhibitions at venues including 36th Bienal de São Paulo (2025); Rockbund Art Museum (2025); TANK Shanghai (2024); West Bund Museum, Shanghai (2023); Seoul Mediacity Biennale (2021); among others. Hao’s works are in the collection of the M+, Hong Kong; Centre Pompidou, Paris; Frac Bretagne, Rennes; the Power Station of Art, Shanghai;, Museu d’Art Contemporani de Barcelona, Barcelona.

Huirong Ye is a doctoral student in East Asian Film and Media Studies at Harvard University. Her current research examines the archivalization and institutionalization of meteorology in modern China, focusing on how it became configured as a mediated domain through audiovisual, technological, textual, and spatial forces, where visibility, legibility, and manageability operate as ideals within evolving regimes of prediction. Her broader interests include environmental humanities, transpacific island and ocean studies, sensory history, activist media, and contemporary art. Huirong holds a BA in History of Art and Architecture and a BS in Journalism from Boston University and earned her Master of Design Studies with distinction from the Harvard Graduate School of Design, where she received the 2024 Design Studies Domain Award.

events.title: 2026 Fall Exhibitions Opening Reception
about: Join us for the opening reception to celebrate two new exhibitions at the List Center: Uri Aran: Look How Hard They Work and Hao Jingban: I Witness.
The opening reception will follow an Artist Talk with exhibiting artist, Hao Jingban, from 5:30-6:30PM.
Exhibiting artists and exhibition curators will be in attendance. Light refreshments and beverages from Momma's Grocery + Wine will be served.

Uri Aran: Look How Hard They Work Uri Aran's work is at once deeply idiosyncratic and oddly familiar: to follow it is to tinker alongside the artist, to be let in on an invention, or perhaps a shorthand between friends. Aran’s first major institutional solo exhibition in the United States gathers a new body of work: annotated panels that hover between quick line drawing and painting, welded sculptures that pose like equations, bulbous forms worked by hand in plasticene and foam, and a mass of piled-up googly eyes—the most elementary form of affect and animation—tragicomically raised to the scale of an earthwork.

Blending documentary sensibility with poetic construction, Hao Jingban makes moving-image installations that are emotionally precise, historically incisive, and formally experimental. Hao’s first major US museum solo gathers recent work centered on I Witness (2025), a three-channel installation that takes up the embodied residue of the COVID-19 pandemic: four participants move slowly through a well-lit apartment, their images punctuated by stories of loss—an older woman who sleeps alone and rises to clean her refrigerator, a group of young people pacing an open field.

events.title: Carrie McKnelly
about: Part of the MIT Fall 2026 Architecture Lecture Series.

Presented with the Design and Computation Group Carrie McKnelly is a design leader whose work sits at the intersection of computational design and material craft. She leads the design team within Nike Innovation's Advanced Digital Creation Studio, spanning footwear, apparel, and accessories, directing digital workflows that embed performance, behavior, and data into how product is imagined, designed, and made.

Carrie holds a Master of Science in Architectural Studies from MIT, studied through the Computation and Design Group, and a Bachelor of Architecture from Pratt Institute. She has taught studio and elective courses at MIT and Pratt, and served as the Howard E. LeFevre Emerging Practitioner Fellow at Ohio State's Knowlton School of Architecture (2015–2016).

Carrie began her career at SOFTlab in New York, designing large-scale installations that revealed the creative potential of pairing computational logic with physical material. At MIT, she explored knit textiles as a material system for complex form and worked alongside the Self-Assembly Lab. She then joined Nike, leading computational design across products including DriFit Advanced for the 2024 Paris Olympics and Athlete Imagined Revolutions, thirteen concepts co-created with athletes and generative AI.
In her current role, she shapes the future of product design through emerging technologies, energized by where computational design and material craft will evolve next.
This lecture will be held in person in the Sidara Auditorium (W41- 1216) and streamed online on YouTube.

events.title: What Are People For: Design Philosophy by Patrick Whitney
about: What Are People For: Design Philosophy by Patrick Whitney Boston-Cambridge Premiere of Gary Hustwit’s New Film and Interactive Design Workshop Join the Morningside Academy of Design for the Boston-Cambridge Premiere of What Are People For: Design Philosophy by Patrick Whitney, the latest short film by acclaimed design documentarian Gary Hutwit (Helvetica, Objectified, Urbanized, Eno), and interactive design workshop on October 24th. Explore how design can address today's most complex challenges from 2-5pm with a hands-on workshop led by Evan Chan and André Nogueira. Chan and Nogueira will introduce the Whole View model, a systems design approach for reframing problems, surfacing the perspectives of diverse stakeholders, and finding new pathways forward in situations where expertise is abundant but fragmented. The session is designed for cross-sector leaders grappling with problems too complex for any one discipline to solve alone.

The workshop will be followed by a screening at 5:30pm of What Are People For. The film is part of a larger multimedia project celebrating the life and work of Patrick Whitney, a pioneering figure in applying design to complex systemic challenges. Whitney's influence on the field has been profound, even as much of his work happened out of the spotlight. This project, produced by Murmur Ring with Ashley Lukasik and André Nogueira, offers a rare opportunity to engage directly with his ideas.

Following the screening, a short panel conversation will start at 6pm, bringing the filmmakers and Patrick together to discuss design's expanding role in addressing complexity. This is a conversation built for a broad audience, regardless of prior design background. The evening will close with a reception, offering time to connect with fellow participants and the project team over refreshments. Together, the workshop, screening, and conversation create a shared foundation for dialogue and collaboration, inaugurating MAD's role as a convening space for systems design at MIT.

events.title: Book Launch: Against Tech Oligarchy
about: In a new book Against Tech Oligarchy, JS Tan — a current DUSP Phd student — writes about tech worker activism, the shifting labor politics of Silicon Valley, and the rise of today's tech oligarchs. In the AI age, as tech's most powerful leaders unilaterally force the new technology upon its workers, this book makes the case that workers — when united — can build the leverage to push back; and even fight for more equitable and socially just ways to use the technology. Join JS Tan and his co-author at this upcoming event for a conversation on these topics and to celebrate the launch of their book.

events.title: Arthur Miller Lecture on Science and Ethics
about: The Program in Science, Technology, and Society invites you to the annual Arthur Miller Lecture in Science and Ethics on Monday, October 26th from 4:00-5:30 pm in the MIT Welcome Center, for a panel lecture on the use of chatbots in children's toys. The panel features Professor Mimi Ito, Director of the Connected Learning Lab, Professor Sherry Turkle, founding director of the MIT Initiative on Technology and Self, and Mike Rizkalla, CEO & Founder of Snorble, a visionary leader in AI, consumer robotics, humanoid robotics, and children's technology.

2027 Arthur Miller Lecture on Science and Ethics There are many views surrounding the advances in children's toys with artificial intelligence capabilities. From a sociological standpoint, some experts believe children should not be the consumers of relational AI, programs that pretend to have a self, capable of humanlike connection. Chatbots draw us into a game of pretend — and for some, pretend empathy becomes empathy enough. While the seductions of pretend empathy are dangerous for all of us, children have no defense; they are first-time learners.

Others in the field view the advent of these new computers, or robots and physical AI, as a chance to change the outcomes we build for ourselves and to realign incentives. Joy, laughter, and love can be something different to everyone. To a child, it is having someone to play with. To a parent, it is five minutes where nothing is going wrong. To a grandparent, it is seeing their family happy.

Embodied AI is a blank canvas. A new mix of cameras, sensors, voice, character, and context gives us a whole new toolkit to do good things, to help people in ways that were never available before. We need to stop running in the other direction and embrace the tech before it becomes weaponized. We need smart, idealistic people leading what comes next, and that is where the smart money should be.

Mimi Ito is a cultural anthropologist, learning scientist, entrepreneur, and an advocate for connected learning—learning that is equity-oriented, centered on youth interest, and socially connected. Her work decodes digital youth culture for parents and educators, offering ways to tap interests and digital media to fuel learning that is engaging, relevant, and social. She is Professor in Residence and John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation Chair in Digital Media and Learning at the…

events.title: Innovation on Steroids:  What are We Learning from the Ukraine War?
about: This event will be offered in person and as a webcast. We will provide the webcast link after you RSVP.

Erik Lin Greenberg, associate professor of political science; co-director, Wargaming Lab, MIT Security Studies Program Erik Lin Greenberg's research examines how emerging military technology affects conflict dynamics and the regulation and use of force. His book, The Remote Revolution: Drones and Modern Statecraft (Cornell University Press), explores how remote warfighting technologies are reshaping international politics. In other ongoing projects, he explores how technology and public opinion influence international politics and decisions on the use of force. He is also interested in the international politics of food and the use of wargaming as a tool of scholarly inquiry. Before entering academia, he was an active duty officer in the United States Air Force and completed assignments in operational units, Headquarters Air Force, and the Joint Staff. events.title: Cities of Islamic Art: From Historical Visual Systems to the Formation of Contemporary Islamic Art in North America
about: This lecture uses Cities of Islamic Art, Vol. 2 as both an object and a methodology to examine Islamic art as a mobile system of visual knowledge rather than a fixed historical style. Beginning with historical surfaces from Isfahan, Istanbul, Damascus, Cairo, and Granada, the talk traces how motifs migrate across ceramics, tiles, manuscripts, and architecture to form the fabric of visual culture and heritage known as “Islamic Art.”

The lecture then shifts to the speaker’s doctoral research, examining how these visual systems are reframed and redefined by visual and sonic artists within the North American diaspora context. The artist’s book functions here as a curatorial and analytical device—a way of reorganizing visual knowledge outside conventional art historical and museological categories.

events.title: MIT Music Tech Speaker Series: Andrew McPherson
about: Enacted, not Extracted: Designing and Performing with Music-Analytical Concepts This is a talk about designing musical instruments and the delicate interplay of artistic and technical ways of thinking. All instruments, and especially digital ones, entail a balance between design and analysis, with instruments relying on symbolic or numerical models of music in order to create it, as exemplified in the venerable MIDI standard. However, no system is ever devoid of sociocultural context, and even the simplest technologies when examined in situ can exhibit fascinating complexity.

This talk will begin with a stubbornly contrarian take on some seemingly obvious premises of musical ontology. Physicist and feminist theorist Karen Barad writes that, "language has been granted too much power." I would like to propose that as designers and researchers, we can let words about music take precedence over the messy and open-ended experience of making music, and that becoming overly preoccupied with language risks propagating clichés and reinforcing cultural stereotypes. Drawing on recent scholarship in human-computer interaction, and science and technology studies, I will recount some alternative approaches and possible futures for designing music technology when technical and cultural factors are inextricably entangled. I will illustrate these ideas with recent projects from the Augmented Instruments Laboratory, with a focus on rich bidirectional couplings between digital and analog electronics, acoustics, and human creative experience.

Andrew McPherson ( is Professor of Design Engineering and Music at Imperial College London, where he leads the Augmented Instruments Laboratory ( a research team creating new musical instruments, studying the encounters between musicians and instruments, and developing high-performance technologies for real-time interactive audio. Andrew received undergraduate degrees in music and electrical engineering from MIT in 2004-05, completing an MEng thesis in the MIT Media Lab and subsequently completing a PhD in music composition at the University of Pennsylvania in 2009. After a postdoctoral fellowship at Drexel University, he joined the Centre for Digital Music at Queen Mary University of London in 2011, moving to Imperial in 2023.

events.title: The Ambivalences of Return: Diasporic Utopias and Anti-Migrant Policies
about: "Return" is a central notion for thinking about the diasporic condition in general (W. Safran). In the "radical imaginations" (R.D.G. Kelley) of the Black Americas of the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries, from Black nationalism to Pan-Africanism, as well as in African anticolonialisms, "return" refers to a shared political dream: making Africa a land of hospitality for all Africans and/or Black people dispersed across the world. Return carries an ideal of reparative justice: reuniting, on the land from which they were torn, those whom slavery and colonization had separated. Within these traditions, however, the idea is fraught with tensions, and for those who experience return to the continent, it often appears as a myth (S. Hartman, M. Condé). In the aftermath of the Second World War, the idea of "return" was elevated to the status of a right. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 recognizes everyone's right to return to their country, and that same year, in the context of the war in Palestine, United Nations General Assembly Resolution 194 affirmed it for Palestinian refugees. From then on, the term became the object of competing claims to the same land, as illustrated two years later by the Israeli Law of Return.

This term, born of the experience of violence and carrying a constantly renewed desire for justice within diasporized communities separated from a homeland, whether real or imagined, takes on a radically antithetical meaning in twenty-first-century migration policies, particularly in Europe. In 2026, in the European Union's "Return Regulation," which complements the Pact on Migration and Asylum, "return" appears as a euphemism for "removal" or "deportation," to a land that is not necessarily the land of origin.

This lecture will therefore examine the antithetical uses of a term that lies at the heart of any reflection on the migratory condition, where reparative diasporic imaginations and contemporary migration and asylum policies in many countries pursuing externalized borders policies invest similar signifiers with contradictory meanings. I will analyze the ambivalences of the term "return," drawing specifically on twentieth-century African and Black diasporic imaginaries and on contemporary European migration policies.

events.title: Anooradha Iyer Siddiqi and Rachel Lee
about: Anooradha Iyer Siddiqi and Rachel Lee Presented with the HTC Forum Part of the MIT Fall 2026 Architecture Lecture Series The Work of Collaboration Collaboration has often occupied an ambiguous place within architectural history, a discipline that continues to privilege individual authorship, singular expertise and archival authority. Collaboration can unsettle these privileges. By bringing researchers together it reshapes the questions we ask, the evidence we value and the histories we are able to write.

Taking the Feminist Architectural Histories of Migration project as a point of departure, we reflect on collaboration as both a feminist practice and a mode of historical inquiry. Drawing on our shared work, as well as subsequent projects developed with artists, designers, archivists, communities and fellow researchers, we consider how collaborative methods have transformed our scholarship.

Rather than presenting collaboration as an exception to scholarly practice, the lecture argues that it is a way of producing more generous, situated and critically engaged architectural histories. Looking back at one collaboration and forward to many others, it asks what kinds of historical knowledge become possible when research is understood as a collective endeavour.

Rachel Lee is Assistant Professor in the Department of Architecture at TU Delft. Her research explores colonial and postcolonial architecture and urbanism, migration, gender and heritage, with a particular interest in how architectural histories are researched, written and shared through archives, collaboration and material culture. Her work spans archival research, oral history, exhibitions and digital publishing, developing collaborative approaches to architectural history. Her work includes Feminist Architectural Histories of Migration, a long-term collaboration with architectural historian Anooradha Siddiqi; Planted!, a collaborative digital archive tracing the global histories of a colonial chair; Sourcery!, a research platform exploring new archival methods and knowledge infrastructures for architectural history; and ongoing research on the architect Otto Koenigsberger.
